I need to think about this year the same way I've thought about every year for the past three decades. I'm 55, my bones know this land, and I don't have time for experiments that might fail. My family has about 10 mu of good flat land in Quzhou, and I need to make sure we have enough to eat and enough cash for my children's needs.

The winter wheat went into the ground last October, like it always does. I sowed Luyuan 502 — it's an improved variety that does well here, and I saved some seed from last year but also bought fresh seed from the shop to make sure the germination is strong. That wheat is sitting on 7 mu, and right now it needs my attention: spring top-dressing with urea, two more irrigations from our well, and a few sprays to keep the diseases and weeds down. I expect about 1000 jin per mu if the weather cooperates.

After we harvest the wheat in early June, I won't waste a single day. I'll plant Denghai 605 maize directly into the wheat stubble without plowing — no-tillage, just like everyone else around here. It's a hybrid seed, so I buy it in packets from the agricultural supply store. One packet per mu is enough. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat because the wheat stubble and roots are still in the soil, and I'll give it two good irrigations in the summer. I should get around 1100 jin per mu.

I also keep 3 mu for cotton. Cotton is hard work — I know I'll be spraying pesticides sixteen times or more — but the price is good and it brings in more cash per mu than maize. I plant 99-1, an improved cotton variety, in early April after rotary tilling the soil. Cotton needs careful management, but my wife and I have done it for years. We expect about 550 jin per mu.

For fertilizer, I follow what the shop recommends and what I've seen work: the wheat gets the most nitrogen because it feeds my family, the maize gets a moderate dose, and the cotton gets balanced fertilizer to support the bolls. I use compound fertilizer as the base and top-dress with urea or ammonium bicarbonate when the crops need a boost. Irrigation comes from our well, and I border-flood the fields because that's what our land is set up for.
